question: To whom does Luke address his orderly account?
answer_choice_2: Timothy
correct_answer: Theophilus
learning_objective: Recall the stated recipient and purpose of Luke’s Gospel.
explanation: Luke writes an orderly account to Theophilus so he may have certainty concerning the things he was taught.
common_misconception: Some assume the Gospels were written anonymously to no one in particular.

question: Which angel announced the births of both John and Jesus?
answer_choice_2: Gabriel
answer_choice_4: An unnamed angel of the Lord
correct_answer: Gabriel
learning_objective: Identify the messenger who brings both birth announcements.
explanation: Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, appears first to Zechariah and then to Mary.
common_misconception: Michael is often confused with Gabriel; Michael is the warrior archangel, not the messenger here.

question: Where was the newborn Jesus laid?
answer_choice_1: In a cradle at the inn
answer_choice_2: In the temple courts
answer_choice_4: In His mother’s arms in a guest room
correct_answer: In a manger
learning_objective: Recall the humble circumstances of Jesus’ birth.
explanation: Mary wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
common_misconception: The familiar stable is an inference; Luke mentions only the manger and the lack of room.

question: Who were the first people told of Jesus’ birth?
answer_choice_2: Wise men from the east
correct_answer: Shepherds in the fields
learning_objective: Recall who received the angelic birth announcement.
explanation: An angel announced good news of great joy to shepherds keeping watch over their flocks by night.
common_misconception: The wise men appear in Matthew, not Luke, and arrived much later.

question: What happened to Zechariah when he doubted Gabriel’s word?
answer_choice_2: He was unable to speak until the child was born
answer_choice_3: He was sent away from the temple
answer_choice_4: He fell into a deep sleep
correct_answer: He was unable to speak until the child was born
learning_objective: Understand the consequence of unbelief in the temple scene.
explanation: Because he did not believe, Zechariah was mute until the day John was named; his tongue was loosed and he blessed God.
common_misconception: Some remember blindness, confusing this with Saul’s experience in Acts.

question: Whose song praises God for lifting up the humble and filling the hungry?
answer_choice_2: Anna’s
correct_answer: Mary’s
learning_objective: Identify the Magnificat and its speaker.
explanation: Mary’s Magnificat magnifies the Lord who scatters the proud, brings down the mighty, and exalts those of humble estate.
common_misconception: Zechariah also sings (the Benedictus, Luke 1:68-79), but the reversal song is Mary’s.

question: Who was promised he would not see death before seeing the Lord’s Christ?
answer_choice_2: Zechariah
correct_answer: Simeon
learning_objective: Recall the righteous man who blessed the infant Jesus in the temple.
explanation: Simeon, righteous and devout, took the child in his arms and blessed God for the salvation prepared before all peoples.
common_misconception: Simeon of Luke 2 is not Simon Peter, who is called later in Luke 5.

question: Where did Mary and Joseph find the twelve-year-old Jesus after three days?
answer_choice_1: On the road home to Nazareth
answer_choice_2: In the temple among the teachers
answer_choice_4: At a relative’s house in Jerusalem
correct_answer: In the temple among the teachers
learning_objective: Recall the only boyhood episode recorded in the Gospels.
explanation: They found Him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions; all were amazed at His understanding.
common_misconception: He was not teaching from authority yet but listening and questioning as a student would.

question: Why does Luke name Caesar Augustus and Quirinius at Jesus’ birth?
answer_choice_2: To anchor the gospel in datable, public history
answer_choice_3: To show Jesus was born a Roman citizen
answer_choice_4: To explain why the shepherds were working
correct_answer: To anchor the gospel in datable, public history
learning_objective: Understand Luke’s historical method.
explanation: Luke repeatedly fixes his account to named rulers and censuses, presenting the gospel as something that happened in real time and place, not as legend.
common_misconception: Some read the rulers as mere scene-setting rather than as Luke’s claim to verifiable history.

question: What does Mary’s Magnificat reveal about how God works?
answer_choice_1: He rewards the powerful who serve Him
answer_choice_2: He remains distant from human affairs
answer_choice_3: He overturns human status, exalting the humble and sending the rich away empty
answer_choice_4: He blesses Israel only, never the nations
correct_answer: He overturns human status, exalting the humble and sending the rich away empty
learning_objective: Grasp the theme of divine reversal that runs through Luke.
explanation: God scatters the proud, brings down rulers, exalts the humble, and fills the hungry — a pattern Luke traces through the whole Gospel.
common_misconception: The song is often heard as gentle piety rather than as the bold announcement of reversal it is.

question: What did Simeon mean when he told Mary a sword would pierce her own soul?
answer_choice_1: She would be persecuted by Herod
answer_choice_2: She would suffer as her Son was opposed and put to death
answer_choice_3: She would lose her other children
answer_choice_4: She would be exiled from Israel
correct_answer: She would suffer as her Son was opposed and put to death
learning_objective: Connect Simeon’s prophecy to the cross.
explanation: Simeon foretells that Jesus will be a sign opposed, causing the fall and rising of many — and that His mother will share the grief of that opposition.
common_misconception: The saying is sometimes read as a general warning rather than a specific foreshadowing of the crucifixion.

question: What does the prophetess Anna add to Luke’s birth account?
answer_choice_1: A rebuke of the temple leadership
answer_choice_2: A second faithful witness who proclaims the child to all awaiting redemption
answer_choice_3: A prediction of the date of Jesus’ death
answer_choice_4: A call for the shepherds to return
correct_answer: A second faithful witness who proclaims the child to all awaiting redemption
learning_objective: See how Luke pairs male and female witnesses to Jesus.
explanation: Anna, an aged widow who never left the temple, gave thanks and spoke of the child to all who waited for the redemption of Jerusalem — pairing with Simeon as a second witness.
common_misconception: Anna is easy to overlook, but Luke deliberately pairs men and women as witnesses throughout.

question: What did John the Baptist proclaim in the region around the Jordan?
answer_choice_1: A baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins
answer_choice_2: The immediate overthrow of Rome
answer_choice_4: The end of the law of Moses
correct_answer: A baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins
learning_objective: Recall the content of John’s preaching.
explanation: John proclaimed a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, preparing the way of the Lord.
common_misconception: John’s baptism is sometimes confused with Christian baptism in the name of Jesus.

question: How far back does Luke trace Jesus’ genealogy?
answer_choice_2: To David
correct_answer: To Adam
learning_objective: Recall the endpoint of Luke’s genealogy.
explanation: Luke traces the line back past Abraham all the way to Adam, the son of God.
common_misconception: Matthew’s genealogy stops at Abraham; Luke’s does not.

question: How long was Jesus tempted by the devil in the wilderness?
answer_choice_2: Seven days
correct_answer: Forty days
learning_objective: Recall the duration of the wilderness temptation.
explanation: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, was led in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil.
common_misconception: The forty days are sometimes shortened to the three recorded temptations.

question: Which prophet’s scroll did Jesus read in the Nazareth synagogue?
answer_choice_2: Isaiah
correct_answer: Isaiah
learning_objective: Recall the text Jesus chose to announce His ministry.
explanation: Jesus was handed the scroll of the prophet Isaiah and read the passage about the Spirit of the Lord anointing Him.
common_misconception: The passage is often attributed to the Psalms rather than to Isaiah 61.

question: How did Jesus answer each of the devil’s temptations?
answer_choice_2: By calling on angels
correct_answer: By quoting Scripture
learning_objective: Observe Jesus’ method of resisting temptation.
explanation: Each time Jesus replies “It is written,” answering the tempter from Deuteronomy.
common_misconception: Jesus did not out-argue the devil with new revelation; He stood on the written word.

question: What did John tell the crowds to do when they asked, “What then shall we do?”
answer_choice_1: Leave their jobs and follow him
answer_choice_2: Fast for forty days
answer_choice_3: Share their extra tunic and food with those who have none
answer_choice_4: Offer a sin offering at the temple
correct_answer: Share their extra tunic and food with those who have none
learning_objective: Understand what John meant by fruit in keeping with repentance.
explanation: John’s answer is concrete and social: whoever has two tunics is to share, and whoever has food is to do likewise.
common_misconception: Repentance is often reduced to feeling sorry rather than changed action.

question: How did Jesus’ hometown react after He said the Scripture was fulfilled that day?
answer_choice_1: They asked Him to stay and teach
answer_choice_2: They were filled with wrath and tried to throw Him off a cliff
answer_choice_3: They ignored Him and went home
answer_choice_4: They brought their sick to be healed
correct_answer: They were filled with wrath and tried to throw Him off a cliff
learning_objective: Recall the outcome of the Nazareth synagogue scene.
explanation: The congregation was driven to rage, drove Him out of town, and meant to throw Him down the hill — but He passed through their midst.
common_misconception: The crowd’s early amazement (v. 22) is often mistaken for acceptance.

question: What did the demons cry out that the crowds had not yet grasped?
answer_choice_1: That He was a prophet like Elijah
answer_choice_2: That He was the Son of God, the Holy One of God
answer_choice_3: That He would rebuild the temple
correct_answer: That He was the Son of God, the Holy One of God
learning_objective: Notice who recognizes Jesus’ identity first in Luke.
explanation: The unclean spirits name Him the Holy One of God and the Son of God, and Jesus rebukes them into silence.
common_misconception: The demons’ accurate confession is not faith — recognition is not the same as trust.

question: Why does Luke’s genealogy run back to Adam rather than stopping at Abraham?
answer_choice_1: To prove Jesus’ legal claim to David’s throne
answer_choice_2: To present Jesus as Savior of the whole human race, not Israel alone
answer_choice_3: To correct an error in Matthew’s list
answer_choice_4: To show Jesus was older than the patriarchs
correct_answer: To present Jesus as Savior of the whole human race, not Israel alone
learning_objective: Connect Luke’s genealogy to his universal theme.
explanation: Luke, writing for a wide audience, ties Jesus to all humanity through Adam — fitting a Gospel that ends with witness to all nations.
common_misconception: Both genealogies are often assumed to make the same point; they emphasize different things.

question: What in Jesus’ Nazareth sermon actually enraged the congregation?
answer_choice_2: He refused to perform miracles there
answer_choice_3: He recalled Elijah being sent to a Sidonian widow and Elisha healing Naaman the Syrian
answer_choice_4: He criticized the synagogue leaders by name
correct_answer: He recalled Elijah being sent to a Sidonian widow and Elisha healing Naaman the Syrian
learning_objective: Identify the specific offense in the Nazareth sermon.
explanation: Jesus pointed to two Old Testament episodes in which God’s mercy went to outsiders rather than to Israel — and that provoked the fury.
common_misconception: The anger is often blamed on the claim of fulfillment alone, but the text places it after the Gentile examples.

question: What does “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” declare about Jesus’ ministry?
answer_choice_1: That He came to condemn the nations
answer_choice_2: That He was anointed to bring good news to the poor, liberty to captives, and sight to the blind
answer_choice_3: That He would reign politically over Israel
answer_choice_4: That His ministry would be limited to Galilee
correct_answer: That He was anointed to bring good news to the poor, liberty to captives, and sight to the blind
learning_objective: State Jesus’ own summary of His mission.
explanation: Jesus reads Isaiah’s anointing text and applies it to Himself, setting the agenda Luke will trace: good news for the poor and freedom for the oppressed.
common_misconception: The passage is often read as poetry about the future rather than as Jesus’ job description.

question: What is significant about where Jesus stopped reading in Isaiah?
answer_choice_1: He stopped before the line about the day of vengeance
answer_choice_2: He read the passage twice
answer_choice_3: He read only the first sentence
answer_choice_4: He skipped the reference to the poor
correct_answer: He stopped before the line about the day of vengeance
learning_objective: Notice the precise limit of the quotation.
explanation: Jesus ends at “the year of the Lord’s favor,” before Isaiah’s “day of vengeance,” then says the Scripture is fulfilled today — marking this as the season of grace.
common_misconception: Readers rarely notice the quotation stops mid-sentence in Isaiah 61:2.

question: What did Simon Peter say after the great catch of fish?
answer_choice_2: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”
correct_answer: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”
learning_objective: Recall Peter’s response to Jesus’ power.
explanation: Overwhelmed by the catch, Peter fell at Jesus’ knees confessing his sinfulness; Jesus answered that he would now catch men.
common_misconception: Peter’s reaction was not excitement over the fish but conviction over himself.

question: Which tax collector did Jesus call from his booth?
answer_choice_2: Matthew Levi
correct_answer: Matthew Levi
learning_objective: Identify the tax collector called in Luke 5.
explanation: Jesus saw Levi sitting at the tax booth and said “Follow me,” and Levi left everything and rose and followed Him.
common_misconception: Zacchaeus is also a tax collector, but his encounter comes much later, in Luke 19.

question: How many apostles did Jesus choose after praying all night?
answer_choice_2: Ten
correct_answer: Twelve
learning_objective: Recall the number of apostles chosen.
explanation: After a night of prayer Jesus called His disciples and chose twelve of them, whom He named apostles.
common_misconception: The seventy-two of Luke 10 are a later, larger sending, not the apostles.

question: What did Jesus command His hearers to do to their enemies?
answer_choice_2: Love them
correct_answer: Love them
learning_objective: Recall the central command of the Sermon on the Plain.
explanation: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.”
common_misconception: The command is often softened to merely tolerating enemies.

question: What did Jesus teach with new wine and old wineskins?
answer_choice_2: New wine must be put into fresh wineskins
answer_choice_3: Wine should not be stored at all
answer_choice_4: Fasting is required of every disciple
correct_answer: New wine must be put into fresh wineskins
learning_objective: Understand the parable answering the question about fasting.
explanation: The new thing Jesus brings cannot simply be poured into old forms; it requires new containers.
common_misconception: The saying is sometimes read as a rejection of everything old rather than of forms that cannot hold the new.

question: What did Jesus do the whole night before choosing the Twelve?
answer_choice_2: Taught in the synagogue
answer_choice_3: Continued in prayer to God on the mountain
correct_answer: Continued in prayer to God on the mountain
learning_objective: Notice Luke’s emphasis on Jesus at prayer before major decisions.
explanation: Luke alone records that Jesus spent the whole night in prayer before naming the Twelve.
common_misconception: Luke repeatedly places prayer before turning points; it is easy to read past.

question: What follows the blessings in Luke’s Sermon on the Plain?
answer_choice_2: The Lord’s Prayer
correct_answer: A series of woes
learning_objective: Recall the structure unique to Luke’s sermon.
explanation: Luke pairs four blessings with four woes — to the rich, the full, those who laugh now, and those spoken well of.
common_misconception: Matthew’s Beatitudes have no woes, so readers often expect blessings only.

question: What did Jesus say about the speck and the log?
answer_choice_2: Judge the speck first
answer_choice_3: Take the log out of your own eye first
answer_choice_4: Ask a third party to judge
correct_answer: Take the log out of your own eye first
learning_objective: Understand Jesus’ teaching on self-examination.
explanation: Only after removing the log from your own eye will you see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s.
common_misconception: The saying forbids hypocritical judging, not all discernment.

question: Why did Jesus cite David eating the bread of the Presence when challenged about the Sabbath?
answer_choice_1: To show the law had been abolished
answer_choice_2: To prove the Pharisees misquoted Scripture
answer_choice_3: To show human need outweighs ritual, and that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath
answer_choice_4: To argue that David was greater than Moses
correct_answer: To show human need outweighs ritual, and that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath
learning_objective: Follow Jesus’ argument about Sabbath authority.
explanation: Jesus appeals to a precedent the Pharisees accepted, then claims an authority greater than the precedent: He is lord of the Sabbath.
common_misconception: The point is not that rules do not matter, but that the Lawgiver Himself is standing in front of them.

question: How does Luke’s “Blessed are you who are poor” differ from Matthew’s wording?
answer_choice_2: Luke speaks directly to the materially poor and adds a matching woe to the rich
correct_answer: Luke speaks directly to the materially poor and adds a matching woe to the rich
learning_objective: Compare the two sermon accounts on this point.
explanation: Luke’s blunt “you who are poor,” set against “woe to you who are rich,” fits his sustained concern for the poor and the reversal of status.
common_misconception: The two accounts are often merged, flattening Luke’s sharper economic edge.

question: What is the point of the two builders at the end of the sermon?
answer_choice_2: Only hearing that becomes doing gives a foundation that stands
answer_choice_3: Houses should be built on high ground
answer_choice_4: Floods are a judgment on the wicked
correct_answer: Only hearing that becomes doing gives a foundation that stands
learning_objective: Grasp the sermon’s closing demand.
explanation: “Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?” Both men heard; only the one who acted stood in the flood.
common_misconception: The parable is often read as being about storms in life rather than about obedience.

question: What does “a good tree bears good fruit” teach?
answer_choice_1: Good deeds make a person good
answer_choice_2: Outward conduct reveals the heart’s true condition
correct_answer: Outward conduct reveals the heart’s true condition
learning_objective: Connect conduct to the condition of the heart.
explanation: “Out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” — words and deeds reveal what is already there rather than creating it.
common_misconception: The order is often reversed, as if doing good deeds could produce a good heart.

question: Whose servant did Jesus heal without entering the house?
answer_choice_2: A centurion’s
correct_answer: A centurion’s
learning_objective: Recall the healing that drew Jesus’ praise for great faith.
explanation: A centurion sent word that Jesus need only say the word; Jesus marveled and said He had not found such faith in Israel.
common_misconception: Jairus, the synagogue ruler, appears later in Luke 8 with his daughter.

question: In what town did Jesus raise a widow’s only son?
answer_choice_2: Capernaum
correct_answer: Nain
learning_objective: Recall the setting of this resurrection account.
explanation: At the gate of Nain Jesus had compassion on a widow burying her only son, and gave him back to his mother.
common_misconception: The raising of Lazarus at Bethany is in John, not Luke.

question: What did the sinful woman do to Jesus’ feet in the Pharisee’s house?
answer_choice_1: Washed them with water from a basin
answer_choice_2: Wet them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them
correct_answer: Wet them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them
learning_objective: Recall the woman’s act of devotion.
explanation: She stood weeping behind Him, wet His feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them with ointment.
common_misconception: This anointing is distinct from Mary of Bethany’s anointing later in the Gospels.

question: What did Jesus do when the storm swamped the boat on the lake?
answer_choice_2: Told the disciples to bail faster
answer_choice_3: Rebuked the wind and the raging waves
answer_choice_4: Waited for the storm to pass
correct_answer: Rebuked the wind and the raging waves
learning_objective: Recall Jesus’ authority over creation.
explanation: Awakened from sleep, He rebuked the wind and the waves; they ceased, and there was calm.
common_misconception: The disciples’ question “Who then is this?” shows they had not yet grasped who was in the boat.

question: What question did John the Baptist send his disciples to ask Jesus?
answer_choice_2: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”
correct_answer: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”
learning_objective: Recall John’s question from prison.
explanation: John, imprisoned, sent two disciples to ask whether Jesus was the coming one; Jesus pointed to the blind seeing and the poor hearing good news.
common_misconception: John’s question is often read as failure rather than as an honest inquiry Jesus answered with evidence.

question: In the parable of the sower, what is the seed?
answer_choice_2: The word of God
correct_answer: The word of God
learning_objective: Recall Jesus’ own interpretation of the parable.
explanation: Jesus explains the parable Himself: “The seed is the word of God.”
common_misconception: The soils, not the seed, account for the different outcomes.

question: What name did the demons in the Gerasene man give?
answer_choice_2: Legion
correct_answer: Legion
learning_objective: Recall the naming of the unclean spirits.
explanation: “Legion,” for many demons had entered him; they begged not to be sent into the abyss.
common_misconception: Beelzebul appears in Luke 11 as a slander against Jesus, not as this name.

question: Who was healed by touching the fringe of Jesus’ garment?
answer_choice_2: A leper
answer_choice_3: A woman with a discharge of blood for twelve years
correct_answer: A woman with a discharge of blood for twelve years
learning_objective: Recall the healing interwoven with Jairus’ story.
explanation: A woman who had suffered twelve years touched the fringe of His garment and was immediately healed; Jesus told her that her faith had made her well.
common_misconception: She was not healed anonymously — Jesus stopped to draw her confession into the open.

question: What does the parable of the two debtors teach about love and forgiveness?
answer_choice_1: Large debts should be repaid first
answer_choice_2: The one forgiven much loves much
answer_choice_3: Forgiveness must be earned by love
answer_choice_4: Only small debts are truly forgiven
correct_answer: The one forgiven much loves much
learning_objective: Connect awareness of sin to depth of love.
explanation: Simon the Pharisee showed little love because he sensed little debt; the woman’s extravagant love flowed from knowing how much she had been forgiven.
common_misconception: The parable is sometimes reversed, as though her love earned the forgiveness rather than following it.

question: What does the seed that fell among thorns represent?
answer_choice_1: Those who never hear the word
answer_choice_2: Those who hear but are choked by cares, riches, and pleasures of life
answer_choice_3: Those who reject the word immediately
answer_choice_4: Those who hear and bear a hundredfold
correct_answer: Those who hear but are choked by cares, riches, and pleasures of life
learning_objective: Identify the danger of the thorny soil.
explanation: These hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
common_misconception: The thorns are not persecution but prosperity and distraction — an easier danger to miss.

question: Why did the Gerasenes ask Jesus to leave after the demoniac was healed?
answer_choice_1: They did not believe the healing
answer_choice_2: They were seized with great fear
answer_choice_3: They wanted the man to stay possessed
correct_answer: They were seized with great fear
learning_objective: Consider the crowd’s response to Jesus’ power.
explanation: Finding the man clothed and in his right mind, the whole region was seized with great fear and asked Jesus to depart from them.
common_misconception: They preferred their familiar arrangement to the presence of the one who had changed it.

question: Who did Jesus say are His mother and brothers?
answer_choice_2: The Twelve apostles
answer_choice_3: Those who hear the word of God and do it
correct_answer: Those who hear the word of God and do it
learning_objective: Understand Jesus’ redefinition of family.
explanation: Told His family was outside, Jesus answered that His mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.
common_misconception: The saying honors obedience, not a rejection of His mother — Mary herself fits the definition.

question: About how many men did Jesus feed with five loaves and two fish?
answer_choice_2: One thousand
correct_answer: Five thousand
learning_objective: Recall the scale of the feeding miracle.
explanation: About five thousand men ate and were satisfied, and twelve baskets of broken pieces were left over.
common_misconception: Luke records only this feeding; the four thousand appear in Matthew and Mark.

question: How did Peter answer when Jesus asked, “Who do you say that I am?”
answer_choice_2: “A prophet like Elijah”
correct_answer: “The Christ of God”
learning_objective: Recall Peter’s confession.
explanation: While the crowds guessed John, Elijah, or an old prophet, Peter answered, “The Christ of God.”
common_misconception: The crowd’s answers are often mixed up with Peter’s.

question: Who appeared with Jesus on the mountain?
answer_choice_2: Moses and Elijah
correct_answer: Moses and Elijah
learning_objective: Recall the two figures at the transfiguration.
explanation: Moses and Elijah appeared in glory, representing the Law and the Prophets, and spoke with Jesus.
common_misconception: Elijah, not Elisha, is the prophet present.

question: What did the voice from the cloud say?
answer_choice_2: “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!”
answer_choice_3: “Fear not, for I am with you.”
correct_answer: “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!”
learning_objective: Recall the Father’s word at the transfiguration.
explanation: The voice identifies Jesus as the chosen Son and commands the disciples to listen to Him.
common_misconception: The command is to listen — not merely to admire the glory.

question: What did Jesus give the Twelve when He sent them out?
answer_choice_1: Money and provisions for the journey
answer_choice_2: Letters of introduction
answer_choice_3: Power and authority over demons and to cure diseases
answer_choice_4: A written copy of His teaching
correct_answer: Power and authority over demons and to cure diseases
learning_objective: Recall the terms of the sending of the Twelve.
explanation: He gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and told them to take nothing for the journey.
common_misconception: They were sent out deliberately unequipped, to depend on God and on hospitality.

question: What did Jesus say a follower must take up?
answer_choice_2: A yoke
correct_answer: His cross daily
learning_objective: Recall Luke’s distinctive wording on cross-bearing.
explanation: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
common_misconception: Luke alone adds “daily,” making it a pattern of life rather than a single act.

question: What were Moses and Elijah discussing with Jesus?
answer_choice_2: His departure, to be accomplished at Jerusalem
correct_answer: His departure, to be accomplished at Jerusalem
learning_objective: Notice the subject of the mountaintop conversation.
explanation: They spoke of His departure — literally His “exodus” — which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
common_misconception: The glory scene points toward the cross, not away from it.

question: What were the disciples arguing about after Jesus foretold His betrayal?
answer_choice_1: Who would sit at His right hand in the kingdom
answer_choice_2: Which of them was the greatest
correct_answer: Which of them was the greatest
learning_objective: Recall the dispute that follows the passion prediction.
explanation: An argument arose as to which of them was the greatest — immediately after Jesus spoke of being delivered into the hands of men.
common_misconception: The specific request for seats of honor is in Mark and Matthew; Luke records a general dispute.

question: What does “whoever would save his life will lose it” mean?
answer_choice_2: Self-preservation forfeits true life, while losing life for Christ’s sake gains it
answer_choice_4: Life has no value apart from suffering
correct_answer: Self-preservation forfeits true life, while losing life for Christ’s sake gains it
learning_objective: Grasp the paradox at the center of discipleship.
explanation: Clinging to one’s own life loses it; surrendering it for Christ’s sake is the only way to keep it — for what does it profit to gain the world and lose oneself?
common_misconception: The saying is not a call to seek suffering but a warning about self-protection.

question: How did Jesus settle the argument about who was greatest?
answer_choice_2: He placed a child by His side and said the least among them is great
answer_choice_3: He rebuked them and sent them away
answer_choice_4: He divided the Twelve into ranks
correct_answer: He placed a child by His side and said the least among them is great
learning_objective: See how Jesus redefines greatness.
explanation: Taking a child — a person of no status — He said that receiving such a one is receiving Him, and that the least among them all is the one who is great.
common_misconception: The lesson concerns status, not childlike innocence.

question: Why is “He set his face to go to Jerusalem” a turning point in Luke?
answer_choice_1: It marks the start of the Galilean ministry
answer_choice_2: It begins the long, deliberate journey toward the cross
answer_choice_3: It records a change of travel plans
answer_choice_4: It signals the end of His public teaching
correct_answer: It begins the long, deliberate journey toward the cross
learning_objective: Identify the hinge of Luke’s structure.
explanation: From here Luke narrates a sustained journey to Jerusalem; Jesus moves toward His death by resolve, not by accident.
common_misconception: The phrase reads as travel detail but marks the Gospel’s major structural turn.

question: What did Jesus mean about the one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back?
answer_choice_2: Divided, backward-looking loyalty is unfit for the kingdom
correct_answer: Divided, backward-looking loyalty is unfit for the kingdom
learning_objective: Understand the cost of following.
explanation: A plowman who looks back cuts a crooked furrow; Jesus warns that half-hearted, hesitating discipleship will not do.
common_misconception: The excuses in view are legitimate duties — which is what makes the demand so sharp.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: How many did Jesus appoint and send ahead of Him two by two?
answer_choice_2: Forty
correct_answer: Seventy-two
learning_objective: Recall the second, larger sending in Luke.
explanation: The Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them ahead of Him into every town He was about to visit.
common_misconception: This sending is separate from the sending of the Twelve in Luke 9.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: Who helped the wounded man on the road to Jericho?
answer_choice_2: A Levite
correct_answer: A Samaritan
learning_objective: Recall the parable of the Good Samaritan.
explanation: A Samaritan — a despised outsider — had compassion, bound the man’s wounds, and paid for his care.
common_misconception: The priest and the Levite both saw the man and passed by on the other side.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: Which sister sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to His teaching?
answer_choice_2: Mary
correct_answer: Mary
learning_objective: Recall the scene at Bethany.
explanation: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and listened, while Martha was distracted with much serving.
common_misconception: Martha’s service was not wrong in itself; her anxiety and complaint were the problem.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What did Jesus teach when a disciple asked Him to teach them to pray?
answer_choice_2: The Lord’s Prayer
correct_answer: The Lord’s Prayer
learning_objective: Recall Luke’s setting for the Lord’s Prayer.
explanation: Jesus gave the prayer beginning “Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come” in response to a disciple’s request.
common_misconception: Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s and arises from a specific request.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What did Jesus tell the lawyer after the parable of the Good Samaritan?
answer_choice_2: “Your faith has saved you.”
correct_answer: “Go, and do likewise.”
learning_objective: Recall the parable’s closing command.
explanation: The lawyer identified the neighbor as “the one who showed him mercy,” and Jesus said, “You go, and do likewise.”
common_misconception: The parable ends in a command, not merely an illustration.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What did Jesus say Mary had chosen?
answer_choice_2: The good portion, which will not be taken away from her
correct_answer: The good portion, which will not be taken away from her
learning_objective: Understand Jesus’ gentle correction of Martha.
explanation: One thing is necessary, and Mary chose the good portion — attention to Jesus Himself — which will not be taken away.
common_misconception: The point is priority, not that hospitality and work are unimportant.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What was the rich fool’s fundamental error?
answer_choice_2: He laid up treasure for himself and was not rich toward God
answer_choice_3: He failed to plan for the harvest
correct_answer: He laid up treasure for himself and was not rich toward God
learning_objective: Identify the parable’s verdict.
explanation: His plans were prudent but godless: that night his soul was required of him, and his goods went to another.
common_misconception: The man is condemned for self-directed hoarding, not for being productive.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What did Jesus say about sparrows and the hairs of your head?
answer_choice_1: That God counts only great things
answer_choice_2: That not one sparrow is forgotten and even the hairs of your head are numbered
answer_choice_3: That birds are of more value than people
correct_answer: That not one sparrow is forgotten and even the hairs of your head are numbered
learning_objective: Recall Jesus’ grounds for fearlessness.
explanation: If God does not forget a single sparrow, and numbers the hairs of your head, then “fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.”
common_misconception: The comfort is God’s detailed knowledge, not a promise that nothing hard will happen.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What made the Samaritan a neighbor when the priest and Levite were not?
answer_choice_1: He knew the wounded man personally
answer_choice_2: He acted in costly mercy across ethnic and religious lines
answer_choice_3: He was required by law to help
answer_choice_4: He reported the crime to the authorities
correct_answer: He acted in costly mercy across ethnic and religious lines
learning_objective: Reframe the lawyer’s question as Jesus does.
explanation: The lawyer asked who qualifies as his neighbor; Jesus redirects him to become a neighbor — through mercy that costs time, money, and status.
common_misconception: The parable does not define a category to love but a way to live.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What is the point of the friend at midnight and “ask, seek, knock”?
answer_choice_1: Prayer wears God down over time
answer_choice_2: God is reluctant and must be persuaded
answer_choice_3: Persistent prayer rests on the Father’s willingness to give good gifts, above all the Holy Spirit
answer_choice_4: Only urgent needs should be prayed for
correct_answer: Persistent prayer rests on the Father’s willingness to give good gifts, above all the Holy Spirit
learning_objective: Understand the argument from lesser to greater.
explanation: If a grudging neighbor and a flawed human father will answer, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.
common_misconception: The parable is a contrast with God, not a comparison to Him.

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What did Jesus condemn in the woes to the Pharisees and lawyers?
answer_choice_2: Neglecting justice and the love of God while keeping outward observance
correct_answer: Neglecting justice and the love of God while keeping outward observance
learning_objective: Identify the substance of the woes.
explanation: They tithed mint and rue while neglecting justice and the love of God — clean outside, full of greed within — and loaded burdens on others.
common_misconception: Jesus does not condemn the tithing itself: “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.”

quiz_title: Week 27 — Luke 10–12 (On the Road with the Savior)
question: What does “to whom much was given, of him much will be required” teach?
answer_choice_2: Greater knowledge and entrustment bring greater accountability
answer_choice_3: God requires the same of everyone
correct_answer: Greater knowledge and entrustment bring greater accountability
learning_objective: Grasp the principle of proportional accountability.
explanation: The servant who knew his master’s will and did not act receives the greater judgment — responsibility scales with what has been entrusted.
common_misconception: The saying is often applied only to money, though Jesus applies it to knowledge and trust.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What did Jesus urge people to strive to enter?
answer_choice_2: The narrow door
correct_answer: The narrow door
learning_objective: Recall Jesus’ answer about who will be saved.
explanation: “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.”
common_misconception: Jesus answers a question about numbers with a call to personal urgency.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What did the shepherd do when one of a hundred sheep was lost?
answer_choice_2: Counted the ninety-nine again
answer_choice_3: Left the ninety-nine and went after the lost one until he found it
answer_choice_4: Sent a hired hand to look
correct_answer: Left the ninety-nine and went after the lost one until he found it
learning_objective: Recall the parable of the lost sheep.
explanation: He goes after the one that is lost until he finds it, then lays it on his shoulders rejoicing.
common_misconception: The shepherd searches personally rather than writing off the loss.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: How many coins did the woman have, and how many did she lose?
answer_choice_2: Twelve; two
correct_answer: Ten; one
learning_objective: Recall the parable of the lost coin.
explanation: Having ten silver coins and losing one, she lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and searches diligently until she finds it.
common_misconception: The three parables of Luke 15 are often blurred together.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What did the father do when he saw the prodigal son still far off?
answer_choice_1: Waited at the door for him
answer_choice_2: Sent a servant to test his sincerity
answer_choice_3: Ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him
correct_answer: Ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him
learning_objective: Recall the father’s reception of the returning son.
explanation: While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, felt compassion, and ran to embrace and kiss him — before the rehearsed speech was finished.
common_misconception: The father does not wait for the confession; he interrupts it with welcome.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: To what did Jesus compare the kingdom of God in Luke 13?
answer_choice_2: A mustard seed and leaven
correct_answer: A mustard seed and leaven
learning_objective: Recall the pair of growth parables.
explanation: The kingdom is like a mustard seed that becomes a tree and like leaven a woman hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened.
common_misconception: Both images stress small, hidden beginnings with pervasive results.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: Whom did the master finally bring into the great banquet?
answer_choice_2: The poor, crippled, blind, and lame from the streets and highways
answer_choice_3: The original invited guests, after they apologized
correct_answer: The poor, crippled, blind, and lame from the streets and highways
learning_objective: Recall the outcome of the parable of the great banquet.
explanation: When the invited made excuses, the master sent his servant to the streets and lanes and then the highways and hedges, so that his house would be filled.
common_misconception: The excuses are ordinary and reasonable — which is the parable’s point.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What two illustrations did Jesus use for counting the cost?
answer_choice_2: A builder estimating a tower and a king weighing whether to go to war
correct_answer: A builder estimating a tower and a king weighing whether to go to war
learning_objective: Recall the two cost-counting images.
explanation: Both a builder and a king sit down first to calculate — so a would-be disciple should weigh what following Jesus will cost.
common_misconception: The passage warns against beginning, not against following.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: Why was the elder brother angry?
answer_choice_1: The younger brother took his inheritance
answer_choice_2: The father celebrated the younger son’s return
answer_choice_3: He was not invited to the feast
correct_answer: The father celebrated the younger son’s return
learning_objective: Recall the parable’s second half.
explanation: He refused to go in, complaining that he had served for years without a young goat, while the son who squandered everything got the fattened calf.
common_misconception: The parable does not end with the younger son’s return; the elder brother is left outside.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What did Jesus mean by “Go and tell that fox” when warned about Herod?
answer_choice_1: He feared Herod and would flee
answer_choice_2: He would continue His work and finish His course, since a prophet must die in Jerusalem
answer_choice_3: He intended to confront Herod directly
answer_choice_4: He was calling Herod cunning but harmless to others
correct_answer: He would continue His work and finish His course, since a prophet must die in Jerusalem
learning_objective: Understand Jesus’ resolve on the road to Jerusalem.
explanation: Neither Herod’s threat nor the warning deters Him: He will cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day finish His course.
common_misconception: The reply is not bravado but determined obedience to a fixed purpose.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What is the lesson of taking the lowest seat at a wedding feast?
answer_choice_2: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the humble exalted
answer_choice_3: Seating rules should be enforced strictly
answer_choice_4: Feasts should have no places of honor
correct_answer: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the humble exalted
learning_objective: Grasp the reversal principle applied to social status.
explanation: Rather than seizing honor, take the lowest place; the host may invite you higher. “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.”
common_misconception: The teaching is not etiquette advice but the kingdom’s pattern of reversal.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: What unites the three parables of Luke 15?
answer_choice_2: Something lost, sought, found, and joy in heaven over one sinner who repents
correct_answer: Something lost, sought, found, and joy in heaven over one sinner who repents
learning_objective: See the common shape of the Luke 15 trilogy.
explanation: Each parable ends in celebration, and twice Jesus states the meaning outright: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
common_misconception: The chapter is often read as three separate lessons rather than one sustained argument.

quiz_title: Week 28 — Luke 13–15 (Parables of the Seeking God)
question: Why does the elder brother matter to the parable’s original hearers?
answer_choice_2: He pictures the grumbling Pharisees and scribes who resented Jesus receiving sinners
correct_answer: He pictures the grumbling Pharisees and scribes who resented Jesus receiving sinners
learning_objective: Connect the parable to the complaint that provoked it.
explanation: Luke 15 opens with Pharisees grumbling that Jesus receives sinners and eats with them; the elder brother holds up a mirror to them, and the story ends with the father still pleading.
common_misconception: Focusing only on the younger son misses whom Jesus was actually addressing.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: Who lay at the rich man’s gate, covered with sores?
answer_choice_2: Lazarus
correct_answer: Lazarus
learning_objective: Recall the named poor man in the parable.
explanation: Lazarus, a poor man covered with sores, longed to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table.
common_misconception: This Lazarus is a figure in a parable, not the Lazarus of Bethany raised in John 11.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: How many lepers were cleansed, and how many returned to thank Jesus?
answer_choice_2: Ten; three
correct_answer: Ten; one
learning_objective: Recall the healing of the ten lepers.
explanation: All ten were cleansed as they went, but only one — a Samaritan — turned back praising God and fell at Jesus’ feet.
common_misconception: All ten obeyed and were healed; only one worshiped.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: Who went home justified — the Pharisee or the tax collector?
answer_choice_2: The tax collector
correct_answer: The tax collector
learning_objective: Recall the outcome of the temple parable.
explanation: The tax collector, who would not lift his eyes and prayed “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” went down to his house justified rather than the other.
common_misconception: The Pharisee’s prayer was factually true about his conduct — and still self-justifying.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: Who climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus?
answer_choice_2: Levi
correct_answer: Zacchaeus
learning_objective: Recall the encounter at Jericho.
explanation: Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector and small in stature, ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree because of the crowd.
common_misconception: Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, distinct from Levi called in Luke 5.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: What did Abraham tell the rich man about warning his five brothers?
answer_choice_1: A messenger would be sent at once
answer_choice_2: They have Moses and the Prophets; they would not be convinced even if someone rose from the dead
answer_choice_4: Lazarus would be permitted to go
correct_answer: They have Moses and the Prophets; they would not be convinced even if someone rose from the dead
learning_objective: Recall the parable’s closing exchange.
explanation: Abraham answers that those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even by a resurrection — a pointed foreshadowing.
common_misconception: The problem named is not lack of evidence but unwillingness to hear.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: What did Jesus say about serving two masters?
answer_choice_2: You cannot serve God and money
answer_choice_3: Only the wealthy face this danger
correct_answer: You cannot serve God and money
learning_objective: Recall Jesus’ statement on divided loyalty.
explanation: “No servant can serve two masters… You cannot serve God and money.” The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, ridiculed Him.
common_misconception: Jesus frames money as a rival master, not merely a tool.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: What did the parable of the persistent widow teach?
answer_choice_2: Always to pray and not lose heart
answer_choice_3: Widows deserve special treatment in court
answer_choice_4: Justice comes only through persistence in the courts
correct_answer: Always to pray and not lose heart
learning_objective: Recall the stated purpose of the parable.
explanation: Luke tells us the point up front: Jesus told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.
common_misconception: The unjust judge is a contrast to God, not a portrait of Him.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: What did Zacchaeus promise to do?
answer_choice_2: Give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold anything he had defrauded
correct_answer: Give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold anything he had defrauded
learning_objective: Recall the evidence of Zacchaeus’ changed heart.
explanation: Standing before the Lord he pledged half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution — far beyond what the law required.
common_misconception: Salvation came to his house that day; the restitution was the fruit, not the price.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: What is the significance of “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost”?
answer_choice_2: It is Luke’s mission statement for Jesus, spoken over a despised tax collector
answer_choice_3: It refers to the future judgment
answer_choice_4: It was said to the Pharisees in the temple
correct_answer: It is Luke’s mission statement for Jesus, spoken over a despised tax collector
learning_objective: Identify the thematic center of Luke’s Gospel.
explanation: Spoken in Zacchaeus’ house while the crowd grumbled, the sentence gathers up the lost sheep, lost coin, and lost son into one purpose statement.
common_misconception: The verse is often quoted apart from the scandal of the setting that gives it force.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: Why did the rich ruler go away sorrowful?
answer_choice_2: He was extremely rich and would not sell all and follow
answer_choice_3: He was forbidden by the law
answer_choice_4: He did not believe Jesus was a teacher
correct_answer: He was extremely rich and would not sell all and follow
learning_objective: Understand the ruler’s specific obstacle.
explanation: He had kept the commandments from his youth, but the one thing he lacked cost more than he would pay; he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
common_misconception: Jesus’ demand was tailored to this man’s particular idol, not a universal rule for all disciples.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: Why did Jesus weep as He approached Jerusalem?
answer_choice_2: The city did not know the time of its visitation, and destruction would follow
correct_answer: The city did not know the time of its visitation, and destruction would follow
learning_objective: Grasp the grief behind the triumphal entry.
explanation: At the height of the praise, Jesus wept over the city, foreseeing its ruin because it did not recognize the time of God’s visitation.
common_misconception: The triumphal entry is often remembered as celebration only; Luke records lament at its center.

quiz_title: Week 29 — Luke 16–19 (Seeking and Saving the Lost)
question: In the parable of the ten minas, what condemned the third servant?
answer_choice_1: He lost the money in trade
answer_choice_2: He gave the money away
answer_choice_3: He hid the mina and did nothing, calling his master severe
correct_answer: He hid the mina and did nothing, calling his master severe
learning_objective: Identify the failure the parable exposes.
explanation: He returned the mina wrapped in a handkerchief, excusing himself by his fear of a severe master; his own words judged him.
common_misconception: The servant is condemned for inaction, not for a poor return.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did the poor widow put into the offering box?
answer_choice_2: Two small copper coins, all she had to live on
correct_answer: Two small copper coins, all she had to live on
learning_objective: Recall the widow’s offering.
explanation: Jesus said she put in more than all the rest, because they gave out of abundance while she gave out of poverty all she had to live on.
common_misconception: The measure Jesus uses is what remains, not what is given.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: Who agreed to betray Jesus to the chief priests?
answer_choice_2: Judas Iscariot
correct_answer: Judas Iscariot
learning_objective: Recall the betrayer.
explanation: Satan entered Judas called Iscariot, one of the Twelve, who conferred with the chief priests about how to betray Him and accepted money.
common_misconception: Peter denied Jesus; Judas betrayed Him — the two are distinct failures.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: How many times did Peter deny Jesus before the rooster crowed?
answer_choice_2: Twice
correct_answer: Three times
learning_objective: Recall Peter’s denial.
explanation: Peter denied Him three times; the rooster crowed, the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
common_misconception: Luke alone records that the Lord looked directly at Peter at that moment.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: Who first found the tomb empty?
answer_choice_2: Roman soldiers
answer_choice_3: The women who had come with Him from Galilee
correct_answer: The women who had come with Him from Galilee
learning_objective: Recall the first witnesses of the empty tomb.
explanation: At early dawn the women — Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and others — came with spices and found the stone rolled away.
common_misconception: Peter ran to the tomb afterward, in response to the women’s report.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did Jesus say about the cup at the Last Supper?
answer_choice_1: “This is the blood of the covenant of Moses.”
answer_choice_2: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”
correct_answer: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”
learning_objective: Recall the words over the cup.
explanation: After supper He took the cup, saying it is the new covenant in His blood, poured out for them.
common_misconception: The words over the cup and the prayer in Gethsemane both mention a cup, but they are different sayings.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did Jesus pray on the Mount of Olives?
answer_choice_1: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
answer_choice_2: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
answer_choice_4: “Into your hands I commit my spirit.”
correct_answer: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
learning_objective: Recall the Gethsemane prayer in Luke.
explanation: In agony He prayed more earnestly, asking that the cup be removed if the Father were willing, yet surrendering to the Father’s will.
common_misconception: The prayer is honest about the dread and still fully submitted — both halves matter.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did Jesus say to the criminal crucified beside Him?
answer_choice_1: “Your sins are forgiven; go in peace.”
answer_choice_2: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”
correct_answer: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”
learning_objective: Recall the promise from the cross.
explanation: To the criminal who asked to be remembered when Jesus came into His kingdom, Jesus answered, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”
common_misconception: Both criminals mocked at first in the other accounts; Luke records one turning in faith.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did Jesus explain to the two disciples on the Emmaus road?
answer_choice_1: The order of events in Jerusalem
answer_choice_2: The things concerning Himself in all the Scriptures, beginning with Moses and the Prophets
correct_answer: The things concerning Himself in all the Scriptures, beginning with Moses and the Prophets
learning_objective: Recall the content of the Emmaus conversation.
explanation: Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself.
common_misconception: The risen Jesus taught the Old Testament rather than simply proving His identity.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did Jesus pray about those who crucified Him?
answer_choice_1: That they be repaid for their deeds
answer_choice_2: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.”
correct_answer: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.”
learning_objective: See the theme of forgiveness carried to the cross.
explanation: Luke alone records this prayer, offered while the soldiers were casting lots for His clothing — the Savior of the lost interceding for His executioners.
common_misconception: The prayer is not a claim that they were innocent, but intercession for the guilty.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: Why is the repentant criminal significant in Luke’s account?
answer_choice_1: He had been a follower of Jesus in secret
answer_choice_2: He shows salvation given by faith alone, at the last hour, to an outsider with nothing to offer
answer_choice_3: He proves that crucifixion atones for sin
correct_answer: He shows salvation given by faith alone, at the last hour, to an outsider with nothing to offer
learning_objective: Connect the scene to Luke’s theme of grace to the outcast.
explanation: A condemned man with no time for restitution or good works is promised paradise on the strength of a plea — the Gospel of the seeking Savior in miniature.
common_misconception: The account is sometimes used to minimize repentance, though the man did confess his guilt and turn to Christ.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did the Emmaus disciples say happened as Jesus opened the Scriptures?
answer_choice_2: Their hearts burned within them
answer_choice_3: They fell asleep on the road
correct_answer: Their hearts burned within them
learning_objective: Recall the disciples’ own account of the encounter.
explanation: “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” They recognized Him in the breaking of bread.
common_misconception: The burning hearts came during the teaching, before they recognized who He was.

quiz_title: Week 30 — Luke 20–24 (The Cross and the Empty Tomb)
question: What did Jesus commission His disciples to proclaim before His ascension?
answer_choice_2: Repentance and forgiveness of sins in His name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem
answer_choice_3: The immediate end of the age
answer_choice_4: A new law for the church
correct_answer: Repentance and forgiveness of sins in His name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem
learning_objective: State the commission that closes Luke and opens Acts.
